title: Aspirin vs Ibuprofen for a Hangover: Which Is Safer?
excerpt: Aspirin or ibuprofen for a hangover? How each one interacts with alcohol, why ibuprofen is usually the better pick, how aspirin compares with Tylenol, and when to see a doctor.
metaDescription: Aspirin or ibuprofen for a hangover? How each interacts with alcohol, which is gentler on your stomach, how aspirin compares to Tylenol, and safe timing.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** if you're a healthy adult with a hangover headache and no stomach, kidney, or bleeding problems, **ibuprofen (Advil, Motrin) is usually the better pick over aspirin.** Both belong to the same family of anti-inflammatory painkillers, called NSAIDs (non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs), and both treat the headache in a similar way. The differences are in the side effects. Aspirin is generally rougher on the stomach at pain-relief doses, and it thins your blood for days rather than hours. After a night of drinking, when alcohol has already irritated your stomach lining, those two traits make aspirin the weaker choice for most people.

**The quick rules:**

- **Wait until the alcohol has cleared.** Don't take either one while drinking or right before bed after a big night.
- **Eat something and drink water first.** Both drugs are harder on an empty, alcohol-irritated stomach.
- **Pick one, not both.** Aspirin and ibuprofen are the same class of drug. Stacking them adds risk, not relief.
- **Use the lowest label dose that helps.** One or two 200 mg ibuprofen tablets, or one or two 325 mg aspirin tablets.
- **If you have 3 or more drinks most days,** talk to a doctor or pharmacist before using either. Both labels carry a stomach-bleeding warning at exactly that threshold.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains how these medicines work and what their labels say. It is not a substitute for a doctor or pharmacist who knows your health history. **Talk to a doctor or pharmacist before taking aspirin or ibuprofen after drinking if** you drink 3 or more drinks most days, have had a stomach ulcer or bleeding, have kidney disease, heart disease, or high blood pressure, take a blood thinner, daily low-dose aspirin, a steroid, or an antidepressant, have asthma that painkillers have triggered before, or are pregnant. **Get emergency help (call 911, or Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 in the US) if** you vomit blood or something that looks like coffee grounds, have black or tarry stools, severe stomach pain, trouble breathing, or think you took more than the labeled dose.

## How Aspirin and Ibuprofen Interact With Alcohol

To pick between them, it helps to know what they share and where they differ.

### What they have in common

Both aspirin and ibuprofen block enzymes called **COX-1 and COX-2** (cyclooxygenase). These enzymes make **prostaglandins**, chemical messengers that drive pain, swelling, and fever. Blocking them is why both drugs ease a headache.

Prostaglandins also do a protective job. In your stomach, they help maintain the mucus layer and blood flow that shield the stomach lining from its own acid. When an NSAID lowers prostaglandins, that shield thins. Alcohol, meanwhile, irritates the stomach lining directly and increases acid. Put the two together and you get the core interaction: **alcohol damages the lining while the NSAID weakens its defenses.** That's why both labels carry the same warning about stomach bleeding for people who have 3 or more alcoholic drinks every day while using the product.

Both drugs also affect the kidneys. Prostaglandins help keep blood flowing to the kidneys, especially when you're short on fluids. After drinking, you often are, since alcohol makes you pee more. A normal dose in a healthy person who rehydrates is rarely a problem, but it's another reason not to take these drugs while you're still dry and drinking.

### Where aspirin is different

Aspirin has two traits that set it apart from ibuprofen:

1. **It thins your blood for days.** Aspirin blocks COX permanently in platelets, the cell fragments that help blood clot. Platelets can't make new enzyme, so the effect lasts until your body replaces them, which takes roughly a week to ten days. Ibuprofen's blocking is temporary and fades as the drug leaves your body, usually within a day. Alcohol also has mild effects on platelets and blood vessels. If you bump your head, cut yourself, or have stomach irritation that starts to bleed, longer-lasting blood thinning makes it worse.
2. **It may raise blood alcohol if taken before or during drinking.** Your stomach has a small amount of the enzyme that starts breaking down alcohol (alcohol dehydrogenase). A study published in *JAMA* in 1990 reported that taking aspirin before drinking led to higher blood alcohol levels than drinking alone, apparently by slowing that stomach enzyme. Later studies have given mixed results, so the size of the effect is uncertain. It's still one more reason not to take aspirin "ahead of time."

### Where ibuprofen is different

Ibuprofen is generally considered one of the gentler NSAIDs on the stomach at standard over-the-counter doses, though it's by no means risk-free. Its effect on blood clotting is short-lived. Its main downsides after drinking are the same stomach and kidney concerns every NSAID shares. For a deeper look at each drug on its own, see our guides to [aspirin and alcohol](/never-hungover/aspirin-and-alcohol) and [ibuprofen and alcohol](/never-hungover/ibuprofen-and-alcohol).

## Aspirin vs Ibuprofen for a Hangover: Side by Side

| | Aspirin | Ibuprofen (Advil, Motrin) |
|---|---|---|
| Drug class | NSAID (also a salicylate) | NSAID |
| Typical adult OTC dose | 325 to 650 mg every 4 hours as needed | 200 to 400 mg every 4 to 6 hours as needed |
| OTC daily limit on the label | Generally 4,000 mg in 24 hours (check your product) | 1,200 mg in 24 hours unless a doctor says otherwise |
| Stomach irritation | Higher at pain-relief doses | Lower, but still real |
| Effect on blood clotting | Lasts about a week or more | Wears off within about a day |
| Effect on blood alcohol | Some evidence it can raise levels if taken before drinking | No similar effect well established |
| Kidney strain when dehydrated | Yes | Yes |
| Alcohol warning on label | Stomach bleeding warning at 3+ drinks a day | Stomach bleeding warning at 3+ drinks a day |
| Not for | Under 19s (Reye's syndrome risk), people with bleeding disorders | People with kidney disease or certain heart conditions without a doctor's OK |

Always follow the label on the specific product you buy. Doses vary between regular-strength, extra-strength, and combination products.

## Which One Should You Take?

Here's a simple way to decide, assuming you've waited for the alcohol to clear and eaten something.

**Choose ibuprofen if:**

- You're a healthy adult with a normal stomach and kidneys.
- You want the least lasting effect on blood clotting.
- You might be playing sports, driving a long way, or doing anything where a bump or cut is possible.

**Choose aspirin only if:**

- Ibuprofen doesn't agree with you and a pharmacist or doctor has said aspirin is fine for you.
- You have no history of ulcers, stomach bleeding, or bleeding disorders, and you're not on a blood thinner.

**Skip both and talk to a pharmacist if:**

- You've had a stomach ulcer, stomach bleeding, or acid reflux that flares after drinking. Our guide to [heartburn after drinking](/never-hungover/heartburn-after-drinking) covers why alcohol aggravates this.
- You have kidney disease, heart failure, or high blood pressure.
- You take warfarin, apixaban, clopidogrel, an SSRI antidepressant, a steroid like prednisone, or a blood pressure medicine such as an ACE inhibitor or diuretic. These raise the bleeding or kidney risk of NSAIDs.
- You have asthma that has ever been triggered by aspirin or other painkillers.
- You drink 3 or more drinks most days.

### A note for people on daily low-dose aspirin

If you take a baby aspirin every day for your heart, don't simply add ibuprofen on a hangover morning without checking first. The FDA has warned that ibuprofen can interfere with the heart-protecting effect of low-dose aspirin if the timing is wrong, because the two compete for the same spot on the platelet enzyme. Your pharmacist can tell you how to space them, or suggest another option. Don't stop or skip your daily aspirin without talking to your doctor.

## Aspirin or Tylenol for a Hangover?

Many people searching this are really choosing between aspirin and Tylenol (acetaminophen). They're very different drugs.

**Tylenol is not an NSAID.** It eases pain and fever but has little anti-inflammatory effect, and it doesn't irritate the stomach or thin the blood the way aspirin does. Its risk sits in the **liver**. A small part of each dose turns into a toxic by-product that the liver has to neutralize, and regular heavy drinking makes that process less safe. Acetaminophen is a leading cause of acute liver failure in the US, often through accidental overdose from taking it in several products at once. We cover the mechanism in detail in our guide to [Tylenol and alcohol](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol).

So the trade-off looks like this:

- **Aspirin:** gentler on the liver, harder on the stomach, thins the blood for days.
- **Tylenol:** gentler on the stomach, no blood thinning, but adds work for the liver.

For an occasional drinker with a healthy stomach and liver, either is reasonable at a single label dose once the alcohol has cleared. If you have a sensitive stomach or are on a blood thinner, Tylenol may suit you better. If you drink heavily on a regular basis or have any liver concerns, ask a doctor before using Tylenol. For many people, ibuprofen ends up being the middle ground: easier on the liver than Tylenol and easier on the stomach than aspirin. Our [Advil or Tylenol for a hangover](/never-hungover/advil-or-tylenol-for-hangover) guide walks through that comparison in full.

## Watch Out for Hidden Aspirin and Doubled-Up NSAIDs

A surprising number of products that people reach for on a rough morning already contain aspirin, ibuprofen, or both kinds of drug.

**Products that contain aspirin:**

- **Original Alka-Seltzer** (aspirin with an antacid)
- **Excedrin** (aspirin, acetaminophen, and caffeine)
- **BC and Goody's powders**
- Some "back and body" and migraine products

**Products that contain ibuprofen or another NSAID:**

- **Advil, Motrin,** and store-brand ibuprofen
- **Advil PM** and other "PM" painkillers, which add a sedating antihistamine
- **Aleve** (naproxen, a longer-acting NSAID)
- Some cold and sinus combination products

Look at the Drug Facts box for the words **aspirin**, **salicylate**, **ibuprofen**, or **naproxen**. If you already took one of these products, you've had your NSAID dose. Don't add another on top.

The "PM" versions deserve their own warning. They add diphenhydramine, a sedating antihistamine. Alcohol is also a sedative, so combining them on a night you drank can leave you much more drowsy and impaired than you expect.

## Can You Take Aspirin or Ibuprofen Before Bed to Prevent a Hangover?

This is one of the most common hangover habits, and it's a poor one. There is no good evidence that taking aspirin or ibuprofen before bed prevents a hangover. What it does do is:

- Put an NSAID on a stomach that's freshly irritated by alcohol, often with no food.
- Add kidney strain at a moment when you're likely dehydrated.
- In the case of aspirin, possibly raise blood alcohol if you're still drinking, and thin your blood right when you're most likely to trip or bump into something.

The research on NSAIDs and hangovers is thin. Small studies decades ago, including one in Finland on a prescription NSAID called tolfenamic acid, suggested anti-inflammatory drugs might ease some hangover symptoms. That fits with the idea that hangovers involve an inflammatory response. But those studies were small, and reviews of hangover treatments have generally concluded that no remedy has strong evidence behind it. A painkiller can take the edge off a headache. It won't fix the nausea, fatigue, or general fog.

If you wake up with a headache, that's the time to take something, after you've eaten and had some water.

## How Long to Wait After Drinking

There's no official waiting time that applies to everyone, so be wary of anyone who gives you an exact number. What's reasonable to say:

- **Your body clears roughly one standard drink per hour**, but that varies a lot with body size, sex, food, and genetics. After a heavy night, alcohol can still be in your blood well into the next morning.
- **If you still feel drunk or can smell alcohol on your breath, wait longer.**
- **Eat first.** Toast, eggs, or anything bland gives the stomach a buffer.
- **Drink water.** Rehydrating takes pressure off the kidneys.
- **Take one label dose, then wait** before considering another. More pills won't fix a headache faster.

## Getting More From a Single Dose

A painkiller works better when you also deal with the other things that make a hangover headache worse.

1. **Rehydrate.** Alcohol makes you lose fluid, and dehydration can make headaches worse. Water, an electrolyte drink, or broth all help.
2. **Eat something.** Low blood sugar can add to the headache and the shaky feeling.
3. **Have a little caffeine if you're a regular coffee drinker.** Caffeine withdrawal adds its own headache. Caffeine can also boost the effect of some painkillers, which is why it's in Excedrin, but too much on a dehydrated stomach can make you jittery.
4. **Rest in a dark, quiet room** if light and noise are bothering you.
5. **Give it time.** Most of the drug's effect shows up within about 30 to 60 minutes.

For more non-drug options, see our guide to [hangover headache relief](/never-hungover/hangover-headache-fast-relief-methods-2025).

## When to See a Doctor

Most hangover headaches fade within a day. A few situations need medical attention instead of another pill.

> **Get emergency help (call 911) if you notice:**
> - Vomiting blood, or vomit that looks like coffee grounds
> - Black, tarry, or bloody stools
> - Severe or worsening stomach pain
> - A sudden, severe headache that feels like the worst of your life, or a headache with confusion, weakness, a stiff neck, or trouble speaking
> - Trouble breathing, wheezing, or swelling of the face or lips after taking aspirin or ibuprofen
> - Signs of alcohol poisoning: confusion, very slow or irregular breathing, seizures, pale or bluish skin, or being hard to wake
> - Shaking, sweating, a racing heart, or seeing or hearing things a day or two after stopping drinking (signs of alcohol withdrawal, which can be serious)
>
> **Call your doctor or Poison Control (1-800-222-1222 in the US) if:** you may have taken more than the labeled dose, you can't keep fluids down for most of a day, you're passing very little urine, or headaches after drinking keep getting worse.

If you find yourself needing a painkiller after most nights out, that's worth mentioning to your doctor. They can look at your full medication list and help you pick the safest option.

## Who Should Be Most Careful

Aspirin and ibuprofen after drinking carry more risk if you:

- Are **over 60**
- Have had a **stomach ulcer or bleeding**
- Have **kidney disease, heart disease, or high blood pressure**
- Take a **blood thinner, daily aspirin, steroid, or SSRI**
- Have **asthma** sensitive to painkillers
- Are **pregnant** (NSAIDs are generally avoided in later pregnancy unless a doctor advises them)
- Drink **3 or more drinks most days** or binge regularly

If any of these apply, a five-minute chat with a pharmacist is the fastest way to get the right answer for you. Our broader guide to [NSAIDs and alcohol](/never-hungover/nsaids-and-alcohol) covers naproxen and the other options too.

## A Better Plan: Fewer Headaches in the First Place

Aspirin and ibuprofen treat a symptom. They don't speed up how fast you clear alcohol or fix the dehydration and poor sleep behind most hangovers. If you're regularly comparing painkillers the morning after, the steps with the best evidence are the simple ones: drink less and slower, alternate alcohol with water, eat before and while drinking, and get real sleep. Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) goes through each one.

Some people also add a supplement. **DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a plant compound studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and the liver. Most of that research is in animals and lab models, with limited human data, so it's promising rather than proven. There is no good evidence that it replaces a painkiller, and it doesn't change any of the safety rules above. If you want to try it, two popular options are [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the lower-cost [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much people take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands.

## The Bottom Line

- For most healthy adults, **ibuprofen is the better hangover choice than aspirin**: gentler on the stomach and its effect on clotting fades within a day.
- **Aspirin** is harder on an alcohol-irritated stomach, thins your blood for about a week, and may raise blood alcohol if taken before drinking.
- **Tylenol** spares the stomach but puts the load on the liver, which matters most for regular heavy drinkers.
- Wait until the alcohol has cleared, eat, drink water, and take **one** label dose of **one** drug.
- Don't take any of them before bed "to prevent" a hangover.
- If you drink 3 or more drinks most days, or have stomach, kidney, heart, or bleeding problems, ask a doctor or pharmacist first.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Is aspirin or ibuprofen better for a hangover?**

For most healthy adults, ibuprofen is the slightly better choice. Both are anti-inflammatory painkillers that work on the same pathway, but ibuprofen is generally gentler on the stomach at normal doses and its effect on blood clotting wears off within a day, while aspirin's lasts for days. Take a single label dose with food and water once the alcohol has cleared. If you have a sensitive stomach, ulcers, kidney problems, or take a blood thinner, ask a pharmacist before using either.

**Is aspirin or Tylenol better for a hangover?**

It depends on which organ you need to protect. Aspirin is harder on the stomach and affects blood clotting; Tylenol (acetaminophen) is easier on the stomach but is processed by the liver, which is a concern after heavy drinking. For an occasional drinker with a healthy stomach, a single dose of either after the alcohol has cleared is reasonable. People who drink 3 or more drinks most days should ask a doctor before using either one.

**Can I take aspirin after drinking alcohol?**

A single standard dose the morning after a few drinks is unlikely to harm a healthy adult, but wait until the alcohol has cleared, eat something first, and drink water. The aspirin label warns that people who have 3 or more alcoholic drinks every day have a higher risk of stomach bleeding. If you have had an ulcer, take a blood thinner, or have asthma triggered by painkillers, avoid it and talk to your doctor.

**Should I take aspirin or ibuprofen before bed to prevent a hangover?**

No. There is no good evidence that taking either painkiller before bed prevents a hangover, and it means putting an anti-inflammatory on a stomach that alcohol has just irritated, often without food, while you're dehydrated. Some research also suggests aspirin taken before or during drinking can raise blood alcohol levels. If you wake up with a headache, treat it then.

**How long after drinking can I take ibuprofen or aspirin?**

There is no official waiting time that fits everyone. A practical rule is to wait until the alcohol is out of your system (the body clears roughly one standard drink per hour, though this varies a lot), then eat, drink water, and take one label dose. After a heavy night, that usually means late morning or later.

**Can I take aspirin and ibuprofen together for a hangover?**

No. They are both NSAIDs, so taking them together roughly stacks the stomach and kidney risks without adding much extra pain relief. Ibuprofen can also interfere with aspirin's effect on platelets, which matters for people who take daily low-dose aspirin for their heart. Pick one, take it at the label dose, and don't combine it with naproxen (Aleve) either.

**Is Alka-Seltzer good for a hangover?**

Original Alka-Seltzer contains aspirin along with an antacid (sodium bicarbonate), so it brings the same stomach and bleeding considerations as aspirin. The antacid can settle an upset stomach, but it does not cancel out aspirin's effect on the stomach lining or blood clotting. Count it as an aspirin dose, and don't add more aspirin or ibuprofen on top.

**Does DHM work better than painkillers for a hangover?**

They do different jobs. Painkillers treat the headache once you have it. DHM is a plant compound studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism, mostly in animal and lab research with limited human data. There is no good evidence that it replaces a pain reliever, and it doesn't change the safety rules for aspirin or ibuprofen after drinking.
